title: Area and perimeter: inside and around

prompts: A rectangular yard is 9 m long and 7 m wide. Find its area and its perimeter, with units.
Draw a triangle inside a rectangle and use it to explain why the area of a triangle is half of base times height.

pedagogy.rationale: Learners count unit squares and trace edges before using the formulas, then fade from a worked solution to guided and independent problems and a composite shape they have not rehearsed.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Multiplies and adds whole numbers, including two-digit by two-digit multiplication.
Knows that a rectangle has two pairs of equal sides and four right angles.

misconceptions.description: Uses the area method to find a perimeter, or the perimeter method to find an area.
misconceptions.response: Contrast the shaded inside with the traced edge on the same shape, and ask which one the question needs.

misconceptions.description: Writes area in metres instead of square metres (or perimeter in square metres).
misconceptions.response: Area counts squares that cover a surface, so it is in square units; perimeter is a length.

misconceptions.description: Adds one length and one width and stops, finding half of the perimeter.
misconceptions.response: Trace the whole edge: a rectangle has two lengths and two widths, so P = 2(l + w).

misconceptions.description: Finds base times height for a triangle and forgets to halve it.
misconceptions.response: Show the triangle inside its rectangle: it fills exactly half.

misconceptions.description: Uses a slanted side as the height of a triangle.
misconceptions.response: The height meets the base at a right angle. A slanted side is longer than the height.

scenes.title: Inside the field, or around it?
scenes.learnerAction: Look at the school field and think about two different questions you could ask about it.

content.body:
The school in Gbarnga is fixing its football field. The groundskeeper needs grass seed to cover the field, and rope to go all the way around it.

Those are two different measurements. Today you will learn which one each job needs, and how to calculate both for rectangles and triangles.

accessibility.textAlternative: A rectangular school field, 90 metres long and 45 metres wide. Grass seed must cover the inside of the field; rope must go around its edge. These need two different measurements: area and perimeter.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Read the scene, then press Continue.

offline.note: The diagram is drawn on the device from the lesson data.

visual.caption: The shaded inside is covered by grass seed. The traced edge is where the rope goes.

scenes.title: Count the squares, trace the edge
scenes.learnerAction: Change the rectangle, count the unit squares inside, and trace its edge.

content.body:
**Area** is how much surface a shape covers. Count the unit squares inside: a 6 m by 4 m rectangle has 6 squares in each of 4 rows, so $6 \times 4 = 24$ square metres.

**Perimeter** is the distance all the way around the edge. Add every side: $6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20$ metres.
keyPoints: Area covers the inside: $A = l \times w$, in square units such as $\text{m}^2$.
Perimeter goes around the edge: $P = 2(l + w)$, in units of length such as m.

accessibility.textAlternative: A 6 metre by 4 metre rectangle on a grid of 1 metre squares. There are 4 rows of 6 squares, so the area is 6 times 4, which is 24 square metres. Going around the edge you pass 6, 4, 6 and 4 metres, so the perimeter is 20 metres. Area equals length times width; perimeter equals two times length plus width.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Use the Grid, Area and Perimeter buttons to change the view; use the length and width sliders with the arrow keys.

offline.note: The model is drawn on the device from the lesson data.

blocks.caption: Area: length times width, in square units.
Perimeter: two lengths and two widths, in units of length.

blocks.title: Which one does the question need?
blocks.text: Covering, painting, planting or tiling a surface needs the **area**. Fencing, edging, framing or walking around needs the **perimeter**.

visual.caption: Change the length and width. The area and perimeter are recalculated from the squares you can count.

scenes.title: Worked solution: the school field
scenes.learnerAction: Reveal each step and watch the diagram show what the step calculates.

content.body: Follow one solution step by step. Notice which part of the diagram each step is about.

accessibility.textAlternative: The field is 90 metres long and 45 metres wide. Area: 90 times 45 is 4,050 square metres, the grass seed needed. Perimeter: 2 times 90 plus 45 is 2 times 135, which is 270 metres, the rope needed. Area is in square metres because it covers the surface; perimeter is in metres because it is a length.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Press Show next step until every step is shown.

offline.note: The worked solution is part of the cached lesson.

blocks.problem: A rectangular field is 90 m long and 45 m wide. How much grass seed area must be covered, and how much rope goes around it?

steps.text: Name the measurements: the length is 90 m and the width is 45 m.
The seed covers the inside, so find the **area**.
The rope goes around the edge, so find the **perimeter**: two lengths and two widths.
Check the units: area covers a surface, so it is in square metres; perimeter is a length, so it is in metres.

scenes.title: Solve with help: the classroom and the garden
scenes.learnerAction: Calculate area and perimeter, using a hint if you need one, and read the feedback on each answer.

content.body: Now you calculate. Hints are here if you need them. Type each answer with its unit.

hints: Draw the rectangle and write the length on two sides and the width on the other two.

accessibility.textAlternative: Problem 1: a classroom floor is 8 metres long and 6 metres wide. Find its area in square metres and its perimeter in metres. Problem 2: a garden is 12 metres long and 5 metres wide. Find the length of fence needed to go all the way around it.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each answer box, type the number and choose the unit, then press Check.

offline.note: Answers are checked on the device.

blocks.prompt: A classroom floor is 8 m long and 6 m wide. The school will tile the floor and put a wooden strip around its edge.

misconceptions.feedback: You added one length and one width, which is only half of the way round. Add all four sides.

hints: Tiles cover the floor: how many rows of 1 m squares, and how many squares in each row?

blocks.prompt: A rectangular vegetable garden is 12 m long and 5 m wide. How much fence goes all the way around it?

misconceptions.feedback: That is one length plus one width. The fence goes along all four sides.

hints: A fence goes around the edge, so you need the perimeter, not the area.

scenes.title: Try it alone: the rice farm
scenes.learnerAction: Solve a new problem without hints, then decide which measurement a real job needs.

content.body: No hints this time. Solve it on your own first; the solution appears after you check your answer.

accessibility.textAlternative: A rectangular rice farm plot in Lofa is 25 metres long and 16 metres wide. Find its area and its perimeter with units. Then decide which measurement Mama Kebeh needs to buy wire to go around the plot.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each answer box, type the number and choose the unit, then press Check; choose one option for the question.

offline.note: Answers are checked on the device.

blocks.prompt: Mama Kebeh's rice plot in Lofa is a rectangle 25 m long and 16 m wide.

items.prompt: Mama Kebeh wants to buy wire to go around her plot to keep goats out. Which measurement tells her how much wire to buy?

options.feedback: Yes. The wire runs along the edge, so she needs the distance around the plot.
The area tells her how much ground the plot covers, for example how much seed to plant. Wire goes around the edge.
One side is not enough: the wire must go along all four sides.

scenes.title: Find the mistake: Musa's perimeter
scenes.learnerAction: Read a worked attempt, find what went wrong, and choose the correctly written answer.

content.body: Good mathematicians check work, including other people's. Find the mistake and say how to fix it.

accessibility.textAlternative: Musa was asked for the perimeter of a room 7 metres long and 3 metres wide. He wrote: P equals 7 times 3 equals 21 square metres. Multiplying finds the area, not the perimeter. The perimeter is 2 times 7 plus 3, which is 20 metres. A second question asks which answer for a 5 metre by 4 metre floor's area is written correctly: 20 square metres.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Choose one option for each question with the arrow keys and Space.

blocks.problem: A room is 7 m long and 3 m wide. Find its perimeter.
blocks.question: What went wrong?

options.text: Musa multiplied, which finds the area. Perimeter adds all four sides.
options.feedback: Yes. $7 \times 3 = 21\ \text{m}^2$ is the area. The perimeter is $2(7 + 3) = 20\ \text{m}$.
Adding one length and one width gives only half of the way round. The room has four sides.

options.text: Nothing is wrong: 21 m² is the perimeter.
options.feedback: A perimeter is a length, so it is never in square metres. Check what multiplying the sides finds.

correction: The perimeter goes around the edge: $P = 2(l + w)$.

items.prompt: A floor is 5 m long and 4 m wide. Which answer for its area is written correctly?

options.feedback: Yes. 20 squares of 1 m by 1 m cover the floor, so the area is 20 square metres.
The number is right, but area counts squares, so the unit is square metres (m²).
18 is the perimeter, $2(5 + 4)$, and a perimeter is in metres. The area is $5 \times 4$.

scenes.title: A triangle is half of a rectangle
scenes.learnerAction: Show the height and the rectangle around the triangle, and see why the triangle is half of it.

content.body:
Draw a rectangle around a triangle, with the same base and height. The triangle fills exactly half of it, so its area is half of base times height.

The **height** is measured at a right angle to the base, not along a slanted side. The **perimeter** of a triangle is still the distance around it: add its three sides.
keyPoints: $A_{\text{triangle}} = \frac{1}{2} b h$, where $h$ is perpendicular to $b$.
$P_{\text{triangle}} = a + b + c$, the three side lengths added.

accessibility.textAlternative: A triangle with a base of 10 centimetres and a perpendicular height of 6 centimetres sits inside a 10 by 6 rectangle. The triangle covers exactly half of the rectangle, so its area is one half times 10 times 6, which is 30 square centimetres. The height meets the base at a right angle; a slanted side is longer than the height. The perimeter of a triangle is the sum of its three sides.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Use the Height, Grid and Area buttons to change the view.

offline.note: The model is drawn on the device.

blocks.caption: Half of base times perpendicular height.
The perimeter adds the three sides. It is not the area formula.

blocks.title: The height is not a slanted side
blocks.text: Measure the height straight up from the base, at a right angle. A slanted side is longer, so using it makes the area too big.

visual.caption: Show the grid to see the rectangle around the triangle: the triangle covers half of its 60 squares.

scenes.title: Worked solution: a sports-day pennant
scenes.learnerAction: Reveal each step and watch the height, area and edge appear on the triangle.

content.body: This pennant flag is a triangle. Watch how the height is used for the area and the three sides for the perimeter.

accessibility.textAlternative: A triangular pennant has a base of 14 centimetres, a perpendicular height of 12 centimetres and slanted sides of 13 and 15 centimetres. Area: one half times 14 times 12 is 84 square centimetres. Perimeter: 13 plus 14 plus 15 is 42 centimetres. The slanted sides are used only for the perimeter.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Press Show next step until every step is shown.

blocks.problem: A triangular pennant has a base of 14 cm and a height of 12 cm. Its slanted sides are 13 cm and 15 cm. Find its area and its perimeter.

steps.text: Find the height: it meets the base at a right angle. Here $h = 12$ cm, not 13 or 15.
Area uses the base and the perpendicular height.
Perimeter adds the three sides. The height is not a side.

scenes.title: Solve with help: a triangular garden bed
scenes.learnerAction: Find the area and perimeter of a triangle, using hints if you need them.

content.body: Use the height for the area and the sides for the perimeter. Check each answer before moving on.

hints: Find the side that meets the base at a right angle: that is the height.

accessibility.textAlternative: A triangular garden bed has a base of 10 metres, a perpendicular height of 12 metres, and two slanted sides of 13 metres each. Find its area in square metres and its perimeter in metres.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each answer box, type the number and choose the unit, then press Check.

blocks.prompt: A triangular garden bed has a base of 10 m and a height of 12 m. Its two slanted sides are 13 m each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is base × height, the whole rectangle around the triangle. The triangle is half of it.
You used the slanted side, 13 m, as the height. The height meets the base at a right angle: it is 12 m.
You added the two slanted sides. The base is a side too: add all three.

hints: Perimeter: add the base and both slanted sides.

scenes.title: Try it alone: the roof gable
scenes.learnerAction: Solve a triangle problem on your own.

content.body: No hints. The solution appears after you check.

accessibility.textAlternative: The triangular end of a house roof, the gable, has a base of 8 metres, a perpendicular height of 3 metres and two sloping sides of 5 metres. Find the area to paint and the length of trim around its edge.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each answer box, type the number and choose the unit, then press Check.

blocks.prompt: The triangular gable of a house in Kakata has a base of 8 m and a height of 3 m. Its sloping sides are 5 m each. It will be painted, with wooden trim around its edge.

misconceptions.feedback: You used the sloping side, 5 m, as the height. The height is the 3 m line at a right angle to the base.

scenes.title: Find the mistake: Kofi's triangle
scenes.learnerAction: Diagnose a mistake in a triangle area calculation.

content.body: Kofi's answer looks reasonable, but one measurement is wrong. Find it.

accessibility.textAlternative: A triangle has a base of 6 centimetres, slanted sides of 5 centimetres and a perpendicular height of 4 centimetres. Kofi wrote: area equals one half times 6 times 5 equals 15 square centimetres. He used the slanted side instead of the height. The area is one half times 6 times 4, which is 12 square centimetres.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Choose one option with the arrow keys and Space.

blocks.problem: A triangle has a base of 6 cm, two slanted sides of 5 cm and a height of 4 cm. Find its area.
blocks.question: What went wrong?

options.text: Kofi used a slanted side (5 cm) instead of the height (4 cm).
options.feedback: Yes. The height meets the base at a right angle. $A = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 4 = 12\ \text{cm}^2$.
Look again: Kofi did multiply by one half. The mistake is in which length he used.

options.text: Kofi should have added the sides: 6 + 5 + 5 = 16.
options.feedback: Adding the sides gives the perimeter, 16 cm, not the area.

scenes.title: Apply it: plan the school grounds
scenes.learnerAction: Solve two new real-world problems: an L-shaped garden and a triangular flower bed.

content.body: These shapes are new. Decide what each job needs, then calculate. Split the L-shape into two rectangles.

accessibility.textAlternative: Problem 1: an L-shaped school garden is made of an 8 metre by 4 metre rectangle with a 3 metre by 5 metre rectangle joined below its left end. Find the area for compost and the length of fence around the whole garden. Problem 2: a triangular flower bed has a base of 16 metres, a height of 6 metres and two sloping sides of 10 metres. Find its area and the length of border stones around it.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Tab to each answer box, type the number and choose the unit, then press Check.

blocks.prompt: The school garden is L-shaped: an 8 m by 4 m rectangle with a 3 m by 5 m rectangle joined below its left end. Compost covers the whole garden and a fence goes around its outside edge.

misconceptions.feedback: 72 is the whole 8 m by 9 m rectangle around the garden. Part of that rectangle is not garden: add the two rectangles instead.
You added the perimeters of both rectangles. The edge where they join is inside the garden, so it gets no fence.

blocks.prompt: A triangular flower bed in front of the school has a base of 16 m and a height of 6 m. Its sloping sides are 10 m each. Soil covers it and border stones go around it.

scenes.title: Remember: inside and around
scenes.learnerAction: Recall the four formulas and use one of them.

content.body: Before the check, say each formula aloud and what it measures.
keyPoints: Area covers a surface, in square units. Perimeter goes around, in units of length.
Triangle: $A = \frac{1}{2} b h$ with a perpendicular height, and $P = a + b + c$.

accessibility.textAlternative: Area covers a surface and is measured in square units; perimeter goes around and is measured in units of length. Rectangle: area equals length times width, perimeter equals two times length plus width. Triangle: area equals one half times base times perpendicular height, perimeter equals the sum of the three sides. A question asks for the perimeter of a square tile with 30 centimetre sides: 120 centimetres.
accessibility.keyboardPath: Choose one option with the arrow keys and Space.

items.prompt: A square floor tile has sides of 30 cm. What is its perimeter?

options.feedback: Yes: four sides of 30 cm, $4 \times 30 = 120$ cm.
That is the area, $30 \times 30$. The perimeter goes around the four sides.
That is two sides. A square has four.
